title: S&P 500 CEO Pay Hits Record $22.8 Million as Musk's Mega-Deals Reshape Boardrooms
excerpt: Average executive compensation soared 21% in 2025 even excluding Elon Musk, as the AFL-CIO's annual Paywatch report documents the widest CEO-to-worker pay gap since tracking began in the 1990s.
body:
• S&P 500 CEO pay averaged $22.8 million in 2025 excluding Musk, up 21% — the highest since the AFL-CIO began tracking in the 1990s. Including Musk's $158 billion Tesla package, the average reached $340.1 million.
  • The CEO-to-worker pay ratio hit 312:1 excluding Musk. Including his Tesla compensation, it reached 5,387:1, as the mean annual wage for U.S. workers rose just 3% to $69,770.
  • Musk-inspired mega-pay packages are proliferating across corporate America, with Welltower's CEO receiving $821 million and Goldman Sachs paying $118.9 million in retention awards.

Average compensation for S&P 500 chief executives surged 21% to $22.8 million in 2025 — the highest level ever recorded — even after stripping out Elon Musk's extraordinary pay package at Tesla, according to the AFL-CIO's widely followed annual Paywatch report released Thursday.

Including Musk's $158 billion restricted stock plan, approved by Tesla shareholders last November, the average ballooned to $340.1 million. The data underscores how Musk's compensation — worth as much as $1 trillion if he hits all performance targets — has reshaped corporate pay expectations across America's largest public companies.

The Musk Effect on Boardrooms

The AFL-CIO attributes the record pay levels not just to strong corporate profits but to a structural shift in how boards think about executive compensation. Musk's deal has normalized what were once unthinkable pay packages, giving compensation committees a new reference point when designing CEO incentive plans.

"Musk's pay changes the dynamic when other CEO compensation plans come up. Boards use it as a reference."

— Fred Redmond, AFL-CIO secretary-treasurer

The trend is visible in a growing number of nine- and ten-figure pay packages. Welltower CEO Shankh Mitra received $821 million in 2025, intended to cover most of his compensation over the coming decade. Goldman Sachs paid CEO David Solomon $118.9 million, including a major retention award. Eight S&P 500 CEOs crossed the $100 million threshold — the most since 2021.

Shareholders have responded with mixed signals. Average support for advisory "say on pay" votes at S&P 500 companies stood at 90.6% through late June. But specific mega-packages drew pushback: only 19% of Welltower shares cast supported Mitra's pay plan, and Goldman Sachs received below-average approval at 71%.

The Widening Pay Gap

The report's most politically charged finding is the expanding gulf between executive and worker compensation. The average CEO-to-worker pay ratio at S&P 500 companies reached 312:1 in 2025, up from 285:1 the previous year. When Musk's Tesla pay is included, the ratio climbed to 5,387:1.

Mean annual wages for all U.S. workers stood at $69,770 as of May 2025, up just 3% from a year earlier, according to the U.S. Labor Department. Workers' wages have been held back by two forces, the AFL-CIO argues: the displacement effects of artificial intelligence and a National Labor Relations Board that organized labor views as hostile to union organizing.

"As we talk to our members, they're pissed off over what's happening to them, and they feel as though they should be more vocal in terms of calling attention to inequality."

— Fred Redmond, AFL-CIO secretary-treasurer

Redmond noted that union representation has hit its highest level in 16 years, a trend he connected directly to the growing pay disparities documented in the report.

Moonshot Pay Plans Spread

A Wall Street Journal analysis found that median CEO pay at S&P 500 companies reached nearly $18 million in 2025 — also a new high. More than half the CEOs in the Journal's ranking received raises of 9.8% or more, and the share earning under $10 million continued to shrink.

The proliferation of so-called "moonshot" pay plans — massive stock or option awards tied to ambitious, multi-year performance targets — is accelerating. While evidence suggests these plans often fail to deliver for either executives or investors, boards are increasingly adopting them preemptively.

Political Implications

Rising executive pay feeds directly into broader political debates about why American workers struggle to afford housing, healthcare, and other necessities. The data arrives as both parties gear up for midterm campaigns that will likely feature economic inequality as a central theme.

Boardroom defenders argue their compensation structures are linked to shareholder value and that investors, including the largest asset managers, overwhelmingly approve them. The AFL-CIO's counter is straightforward: the gap between C-suite wealth and worker wages has grown too wide to justify on performance grounds alone.
nri_angle: The widening CEO-to-worker pay gap directly affects Indian American tech and corporate workers, many of whom work at S&P 500 companies where executive pay has surged while employee compensation growth has lagged.
